The experiments were conducted in a 15 cm x 5 cm thin sample of a dilute alloy of succinonitrile, a plastic crystal.
The sample depth was 150 µm, allowing for a single microstructure layer to be visualized.
The thermal gradients used were 70 or 140 K/cm, and the solidification velocities ranged up to 50 µm/s.
The flow was induced by a thermosiphon, allowing for controlled flows from one side of the sample to the other with amplitudes up to 1500 µm/s.
At low flow velocities, downstream inclination of cells and dendrites, as well as asymmetric sidebranching, were observed.
The inclination angle increased linearly with the ratio of flow velocity to growth velocity, with a prefactor of approximately 0.18.
The two types of waves observed had different velocities and profiles: a slow wave with a smooth, quasi-sinusoidal modulation, and a rapid wave with a sharp asymmetric profile.
The rapid waves showed a velocity that linearly increased with the flow intensity, while the slow waves had a nearly constant velocity of about 40 µm/s.
Both waves shared the same evolution of wavelength, which increased linearly with the ratio of wave velocity to growth velocity.
The distance δ = VT, where V is the growth velocity and T is the wave period, was found to be a constant of the material, around 350 µm.
Increasing the sample depth up to a factor of 3 did not significantly affect the observed inclinations and waves.

The authors suggest that the repetitive striations induced by the interfacial waves could provide large-scale structurations of the solid phase that could be controlled or provoked by the flow magnitude.
The authors propose that the major effect of the flow is the solute advection ahead of the microstructure tips, rather than the penetration of the flow behind the tips.

The difference in flow structure between the thin samples (Poiseuille flow) and large volumes (constant flow) could result in weaker flow on the microstructure sides in the thin samples, but the main effect of solute advection should remain the same.

The authors state that the clearest signature of the effects observed in the thin samples would be the repetitive striations in the solid phase, which could be evidenced by post-mortem analysis in large volumes.
